entities.name: The Buddhist Pali Canon (Tipitaka)
entities.label: Text
entities.summary:
The Tipitaka ("Three Baskets") is the complete canon of Theravada Buddhism, the oldest surviving school of Buddhism, preserved in the Pali language and consisting of three major divisions: (1) the Vinaya Pitaka — monastic rules governing the Sangha (community of monks and nuns), with 227 rules for monks and 311 for nuns; (2) the Sutta Pitaka — discourses of the Buddha organized in five Nikayas (Digha, Majjhima, Samyutta, Anguttara, Khuddaka), containing the core teachings on the Four Noble Truths, the Eightfold Path, dependent origination, emptiness, and meditation; and (3) the Abhidhamma Pitaka — systematic philosophical and psychological analysis of reality. First committed to writing in Sri Lanka at the Fourth Buddhist Council (c.

29 BCE) after centuries of oral transmission, the Pali Canon is approximately 40 volumes in printed form — making it roughly 11 times the length of the Bible. It is the primary scriptural authority for approximately 150 million Theravada Buddhists in Sri Lanka, Myanmar, Thailand, Laos, and Cambodia.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: The Buddhist Pali Canon preserved Theravada Buddhism's core teachings and played a crucial role in shaping the spiritual landscape of South Asia for centuries. Its written compilation at the Fourth Buddhist Council significantly influenced the development of Buddhist thought and practice.
